c.tagline: Big Texas ambition — arts, sports, barbecue and JFK history under a wide sky.

taxi.fareNote: Metered cabs start around $2.25 plus per-mile charges; Uber and Lyft are far more common and usually cheaper, especially for the long ride from DFW.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; 311 is the city's non-emergency line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution in parts of South Dallas; tourist areas fine

hood_desc: The high-rise core holding Dealey Plaza and the Sixth Floor Museum, the Arts District, Klyde Warren Park and Main Street Garden; best for first-timers wanting sights, museums and DART light rail at the door.
The walkable, upscale district along McKinney Avenue with the vintage M-Line trolley, buzzing bars and restaurants and the leafy Katy Trail; a favorite base for nightlife and dining.
The historic entertainment quarter just east of downtown, packed with live-music venues, murals, breweries and late-night eateries; suits travelers chasing arts and nightlife.
A walkable Oak Cliff enclave of indie boutiques, galleries, coffee shops and acclaimed restaurants in restored 1930s storefronts; a hipster-leaning local favorite south of the river.
A stylish shopping-and-dining strip straddling Central Expressway, with designer stores, patios and a relaxed, moneyed feel; good for shopping and a quieter stay near Uptown.
lodging: Home2 Suites by Hilton Dallas Downtown at Baylor
La Quinta Inn by Wyndham Dallas Uptown

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the metro area.

sys.n: DART Light Rail (Red, Blue, Green, Orange, Silver Lines)
Trinity Railway Express (TRE) to Fort Worth

transit.pay: Buy fares in the DART GoPass app, from station machines, or tap a contactless card; a single local ride is about $2.50 and a day pass $6, covering DART trains, buses, the streetcar and the TRE within the zone. The M-Line Trolley through Uptown is free.
transit.hours: DART light rail runs roughly 4am to midnight (later on weekends on some lines); buses vary and there is no 24-hour service, so rideshare fills the overnight gap.
transit.note: DART runs one of the largest US light-rail networks by length; the Orange Line reaches DFW Airport and the free McKinney Avenue Trolley loops through Uptown, but Dallas remains largely car-oriented and many neighborhoods are best reached by car or rideshare.

train: Trinity Railway Express to Fort Worth

transit.m: DART Orange Line light rail to downtown (~60 min)
TRE commuter rail via CentrePort/DFW Airport station

tip.r: ~18-20% at restaurants and bars is expected; $1-2 per drink and a few dollars for taxis and hotel staff are standard.

food.name: Texas brisket
food.desc: Post-oak-smoked beef brisket rubbed simply with salt and pepper, sliced fatty or lean and served on butcher paper with pickles and onion.

places.name: Pecan Lodge
places.note: The most celebrated brisket inside Dallas city limits; go early, the line forms before opening.

places.name: Cattleack Barbeque
places.note: Weekday-only smokehouse that Texas barbecue critics rank among the state's very best.

places.name: Terry Black's Barbecue
places.note: Austin family's Dallas outpost; big cafeteria line, reliable fatty brisket and beef ribs.

food.name: Tex-Mex fajitas
food.desc: Marinated skirt steak or chicken grilled and served sizzling with peppers, onions, flour tortillas, guacamole and pico de gallo.

places.name: Mia's Tex-Mex
places.note: Dallas legend where deals get done over brisket tacos and fajita platters.

places.name: El Fenix
places.note: Founded 1918 and credited with codifying the Tex-Mex combination plate in Dallas.

places.name: Herrera's Cafe
places.note: Family-run since 1971; unpretentious plates and a devoted local following.

food.name: Frito pie
food.desc: A split bag or bowl of Fritos smothered in Texas chili, shredded cheddar, raw onion and jalapenos, eaten with a plastic fork.

places.name: Slow Bone
places.note: Chili made from their own smoked brisket; repeatedly named the city's best Frito pie.

places.name: Rodeo Goat
places.note: Burger bar on the west side that serves a heavily loaded Frito pie alongside the patties.

places.name: Terry Black's Barbecue
places.note: Barbecue-chili version on the side-dish line, easy to add to a brisket tray.

food.name: Kolache
food.desc: Czech-Texan pastry: soft sweet dough around fruit or poppy seed, or the savory klobasnek stuffed with sausage, cheese and jalapeno.

places.name: Village Baking Co.
places.note: Artisan Dallas bakery whose morning kolaches sell out; also excellent croissants and bread.

places.name: iHeart Kolache
places.note: Dedicated kolache cafe on Midway Road baking sweet and savory versions fresh daily.

places.name: The Kolache Bake Shop
places.note: Specialist shop known for sausage-and-cheese klobasneks and fruit kolaches.

food.name: Chicken-fried steak
food.desc: Tenderized beef cutlet battered, deep fried and drowned in black-pepper cream gravy, with mashed potatoes and green beans.

places.name: Bubba's Cooks Country
places.note: Drive-through country kitchen near SMU turning out a benchmark chicken-fried steak.

places.name: Norma's Cafe
places.note: Diner open since 1956; chicken-fried steak, cream gravy and mile-high meringue pie.

places.name: AllGood Cafe
places.note: Texas roadhouse cooking with live music; a reliable Deep Ellum breakfast and lunch stop.

food.name: Al pastor tacos
food.desc: Chile-marinated pork shaved off a vertical trompo onto small corn tortillas with pineapple, onion, cilantro and salsa.

places.name: Trompo
places.note: Carves pork straight off the spit; the taqueria that put Dallas trompo on the map.

places.name: El Come Taco
places.note: Mexico City-style taqueria on Fitzhugh, praised for al pastor and campechano.

places.name: Revolver Taco Lounge
places.note: Michoacan-rooted kitchen with handmade tortillas and a chef's-table tasting room.

food.name: Frozen margarita
food.desc: Slushy lime-and-tequila cocktail; the frozen margarita machine was invented in Dallas in 1971 and is now a Tex-Mex table ritual.

places.name: Mariano's Hacienda
places.note: Where Mariano Martinez built the first frozen margarita machine; still serving them.

places.name: Mi Cocina
places.note: Home of the Mambo Taxi, a frozen margarita spiked with sangria swirl.

places.name: El Fenix
places.note: Century-old Tex-Mex house pouring classic frozen and rocks margaritas.

food.name: North Texas craft beer
food.desc: Dallas has a dense brewery scene, from hoppy Texas pale ales to lagers built for the heat, usually poured in warehouse taprooms.

places.name: Deep Ellum Brewing Company
places.note: The brewery that kick-started the modern Dallas beer scene; large taproom and tours.

places.name: Peticolas Brewing Company
places.note: Small-batch brewery best known for the Velvet Hammer imperial red ale.

places.name: Community Beer Co.
places.note: Award-winning taproom with a big patio, food trucks and year-round Texas lagers.

landmarks: Reunion Tower
Dallas's iconic geodesic-domed observation tower lit up at night, offering 360-degree views of the skyline from the GeO-Deck.
Dallas Pioneer Plaza
A sprawling downtown park featuring the largest bronze cattle-drive sculpture in the world, evoking Dallas's cowboy heritage.
The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza
The former Texas School Book Depository overlooking Dealey Plaza, marking the site of President Kennedy's assassination and a place of deep historical significance.
Dallas Museum of Art
A striking modernist museum anchoring the Dallas Arts District with an extensive collection spanning ancient to contemporary art.
Nasher Sculpture Center
A serene indoor-outdoor gallery showcasing world-class modern sculpture amid lush landscaped gardens in the heart of downtown.
Dallas Arboretum and Botanical Garden
Sweeping gardens on the shores of White Rock Lake famous for seasonal floral displays and colorful pumpkin and tulip festivals.
Klyde Warren Park
An innovative deck park built over a freeway, stitching downtown to Uptown with lively lawns, food trucks, and public art.
Fair Park
A National Historic Landmark showcasing the largest collection of 1930s Art Deco exposition architecture in the U.S., home to the State Fair of Texas.
Bishop Arts District
A colorful, walkable historic neighborhood of murals, boutiques, and eateries that captures Dallas's eclectic, artsy side.
AT&T Stadium
The gleaming, retractable-roof home of the Dallas Cowboys, an architectural marvel and a bucket-list stop for sports fans.

train.note: Amtrak's daily Texas Eagle is the only intercity train, calling at Dallas Union Station on the southwest edge of downtown - northbound to Fort Worth, Little Rock, St Louis and Chicago, southbound to Austin and San Antonio, with through cars to Los Angeles on the Sunset Limited three days a week. Union Station is also a DART light rail stop and the eastern end of the Trinity Railway Express commuter line to Fort Worth, which is much faster than the Amtrak hop. There are no passenger trains to Mexico anywhere in Texas. For most Texas city pairs the coach or a flight beats the once-daily train.

intl.to: Monterrey, San Luis Potosi, Guadalajara, Morelia & central Mexico

bus.note: Dallas is one of the strongest cross-border coach markets in the country - Tornado Bus Company alone runs two Dallas terminals with departures deep into central Mexico, and Greyhound serves Monterrey and Nuevo Laredo. Bring a passport and buy a Mexican FMM tourist card at the border crossing; the ride to Monterrey takes roughly 12 hours. Domestic coaches on Greyhound, FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) run frequently to Fort Worth, Austin (about four hours), Houston (four to five) and San Antonio (five). Book online rather than at the counter for the cheap fares.

ferry.note: Dallas is around 300 miles from the Gulf of Mexico and has no passenger ferries; boating is limited to recreation on White Rock Lake, Lake Ray Hubbard and Lake Lewisville.

half.name: Fort Worth
half.blurb: Cowtown neighbor with the historic Stockyards District, daily cattle drives, and a walkable downtown Sundance Square.

half.name: Waco
half.blurb: Central Texas city home to Magnolia Market at the Silos and the Dr Pepper Museum, along the Brazos River.

half.name: Grapevine
half.blurb: Wine-country town on Lake Grapevine with a historic Main Street lined with tasting rooms and small wineries.
